prompt: Which attribute sets a CSS class in JSX?

options.text: className
options.why: "class" is a reserved word in JavaScript, and JSX is JavaScript, so React uses className instead.

options.text: class
options.why: This is the HTML name. In JSX it clashes with the JavaScript keyword, so React renamed it.

options.text: cssClass
options.why: No framework uses this name. It is not part of JSX.

options.text: styleClass
options.why: Not a React attribute. style in React takes an object of CSS properties, which is a different thing.

hint: One HTML attribute name is already a JavaScript keyword.

prompt: Why does this component fail?

options.text: A component must return one top level element
options.why: return can only hand back one value. Wrap the two in a <div>, or in an empty <> </> fragment if you do not want an extra tag.

options.text: cannot follow
options.why: That order is perfectly normal HTML. The problem is that nothing wraps them.

options.text: The text needs to be in braces
options.why: Plain text inside a tag needs no braces. Braces are for JavaScript expressions.

options.text: The function name must be lowercase
options.why: The opposite. A component name must start with a CAPITAL, or React treats it as an HTML tag.

hint: Count how many things the return gives back.

prompt: How do you show the value of a variable called name inside JSX?

options.text: {name}
options.why: Single curly braces drop a JavaScript expression into JSX. Anything inside them is evaluated and the result is shown.

options.text: {{name}}
options.why: Double braces are the Vue and Angular style. In JSX they mean an object inside an expression, which is how style={{color:"red"}} works.

options.text: ${name}
options.why: That is template-string syntax, and it only works inside back ticks.

options.text: <%= name %>
options.why: That is an old server template style, not JSX.

hint: How many braces?

prompt: Why must a React component name start with a capital letter?

options.text: A lowercase name is treated as a plain HTML tag
options.why: React decides by the first letter. <button> means the real HTML button; <Button> means your component.

options.text: It is only a style convention with no effect
options.why: It genuinely changes what React renders, so it is a rule, not a preference.

options.text: JavaScript requires capitals for functions
options.why: JavaScript has no such rule. This one comes from JSX.

options.text: It makes the component faster
options.why: Naming has no effect on speed.

hint: How does React tell <button> from <Button>?

prompt: What is true about props?

options.text: A component must not change its own props
options.why: Props belong to the parent that passed them. A child that rewrote them would make the data flow impossible to follow, so React treats them as read only.

options.text: A component changes props to update the screen
options.why: That is what state is for. To change a prop, the PARENT has to pass a new value.

options.text: Props can only be strings
options.why: A prop can be any value: a number, an object, an array, even a function.

options.text: Props are shared by every component
options.why: They are passed from one parent to one child. Nothing is global about them.

hint: Who owns the value, the parent or the child?

prompt: What is the difference between state and props?

options.text: State belongs to the component and can change; props come from the parent
options.why: State is the component’s own memory and it may update it. Props are handed in from outside and the component only reads them.

options.text: State comes from the parent and props are internal
options.why: The two are the wrong way round.

options.text: They are the same thing with different names
options.why: Who owns the value and who may change it are different for each, which is the whole distinction.

options.text: State is for text and props are for numbers
options.why: Both hold any kind of value. The difference is ownership, not type.

hint: Which one can the component itself change?

prompt: What does useState return?

options.text: An array of the current value and a function to set it
options.why: That is why you write const [n, setN] = useState(0). The square brackets are array destructuring.

options.text: Just the current value
options.why: Then you would have no way to change it. The setter is the second half.

options.text: An object with value and setValue keys
options.why: It returns an array, which is why the brackets are square and you can name the two parts anything you like.

options.text: A function you call to read the value
options.why: The value is handed to you directly. Only the setter is a function.

hint: Why are the brackets square and not curly?

prompt: After calling setN(5), what does n hold on the very next line?

options.text: The old value, because the new one only appears on the next render
options.why: n is a constant captured for THIS render. Setting state asks React to render again, and the new value only exists in that next run.

options.text: 5, the value is updated at once
options.why: If it changed in place, n could not be a const. React re-renders instead of editing the variable.

options.text: undefined until the render finishes
options.why: n keeps its current value. Nothing is cleared.

options.text: It depends on whether the component is async
options.why: This behaviour is the same in every component. It is about rendering, not about async.

hint: n is declared with const. Can a const change?

prompt: Why write setN((old) => old + 1) instead of setN(n + 1)?

options.text: It uses the latest value, so several updates in a row all count
options.why: n is frozen for this render, so calling setN(n + 1) twice adds one in total. The function form is handed the newest value each time, so it adds two.

options.text: It is faster
options.why: Speed is the same. The difference is correctness when updates stack up.

options.text: It is the only form React allows
options.why: Both forms are allowed. The plain one is fine when you are not building on the old value.

options.text: It avoids a re-render
options.why: Both forms cause a re-render. That is the point of setting state.

hint: What happens if you call it twice in one handler?

prompt: What is the key prop for when rendering a list?

options.text: It lets React tell which item is which between renders
options.why: With a stable key React can move or keep a row instead of rebuilding it, so its DOM state, such as a half-typed input, survives.

options.text: It sets the order the items appear in
options.why: The order comes from the array. The key only identifies items.

options.text: It is the id used for CSS styling
options.why: The key never reaches the DOM. You cannot select it in CSS.

options.text: It is required by JavaScript for arrays
options.why: JavaScript has no such rule. The warning comes from React.

hint: React needs to match old rows to new rows. How?

prompt: Why is using the array index as a key a problem?

options.text: If the list is reordered or an item is removed, the index points at a different item
options.why: React thinks row 0 is still row 0, so it keeps the old DOM for new data. Typed input and focus end up attached to the wrong row.

options.text: Indexes are numbers and keys must be strings
options.why: A number is a fine key. React converts it.

options.text: It makes the list render twice
options.why: The number of renders does not change. What changes is which DOM node is reused.

options.text: Indexes are not unique
options.why: Within one list they are unique. The trouble is that they are not STABLE when the list changes.

hint: What happens to index 0 when you delete the first item?

prompt: When does an effect with an empty dependency array run?

options.text: Once, after the first render
options.why: The array lists what the effect depends on. An empty list means nothing can change, so there is never a reason to run it again.

options.text: After every render
options.why: That is what you get by leaving the array out ALTOGETHER. An empty array is different from no array.

options.text: Never
options.why: It still runs the first time. The array controls repeats, not the first run.

options.text: Before the first render
options.why: An effect always runs AFTER the screen is painted. That is why it is called an effect.

hint: No array, empty array and a filled array are three different things.

prompt: What happens if you leave out the dependency array completely?

options.text: The effect runs after every render
options.why: With no list React cannot tell what matters, so it assumes everything does. If the effect also sets state, this is the classic infinite loop.

options.text: The effect runs once
options.why: That is an EMPTY array. Leaving it out is the opposite.

options.text: The effect never runs
options.why: It runs more often, not less.

options.text: React throws an error
options.why: It is valid code. React will not stop you, which is what makes the loop easy to write by accident.

hint: Missing array and empty array are opposites.

prompt: What is the function you return from useEffect for?

options.text: Cleanup: it runs before the next effect and when the component is removed
options.why: It is where you clear a timer or remove a listener. Without it those pile up every render and leak.

options.text: It is the value the effect produces
options.why: An effect returns nothing useful to React except the cleanup. Use state if you need a value.

options.text: It runs before the effect does
options.why: On the FIRST run there is nothing to clean up, so it cannot run before.

options.text: It decides whether the effect runs again
options.why: The dependency array decides that.

hint: What needs undoing when a component disappears?

prompt: A list has 0 items. What does {items.length && <List />} render?

options.text: The number 0 on the page
options.why: && returns its LEFT side when that side is falsy, and 0 is falsy. React then renders the number 0 as text. Write items.length > 0 && ... instead.

options.text: Nothing
options.why: That is what you expected, and the reason this trap catches people. React hides false and null, but it does NOT hide 0.

options.text: The List component
options.why: && stops at the falsy left side and never reaches the right.

options.text: The word false
options.why: The left side is the number 0, not the boolean false, and React does print 0.

hint: What value does && return when the left side is falsy?

prompt: What is wrong with onClick={handle()}?

options.text: It calls handle during render instead of on click
options.why: The parentheses run it immediately and pass its RESULT as the handler. Write onClick={handle}, or onClick={() => handle(x)} if you need an argument.

options.text: Nothing, this is the normal way
options.why: The normal way has no parentheses. With them, the click handler is whatever handle returned, usually undefined.

options.text: onClick must be lowercase
options.why: In JSX it is camelCase, so onClick is right. The lowercase onclick is the plain HTML spelling.

options.text: Handlers must be arrow functions
options.why: A named function is fine. The problem is the parentheses, not the kind of function.

hint: What do the brackets after a function name do?

prompt: An input has value={text} but no onChange. What happens?

options.text: You cannot type in it, because React keeps resetting it to text
options.why: Setting value makes React the owner of the field. Without onChange nothing updates the state, so every keystroke is painted over.

options.text: It works normally
options.why: A value with no onChange is the classic frozen input. React even warns about it.

options.text: The input disappears
options.why: It renders fine. It just will not accept typing.

options.text: React throws an error
options.why: It is a console warning, not an error. The page keeps running.

hint: If React sets the value every render, what happens to what you typed?

prompt: What is <> </> in JSX?

options.text: A fragment: it groups elements without adding a real tag
options.why: It satisfies the one-root rule without putting an extra <div> in the DOM, which matters when a stray div would break a CSS grid or a table.

options.text: A comment
options.why: A JSX comment is {/* like this */}.

options.text: An empty div
options.why: A div WOULD appear in the HTML. The point of a fragment is that nothing appears.

options.text: A placeholder for a missing component
options.why: It is a real feature, not a placeholder.

hint: What is in the HTML afterwards?

prompt: Why is items.push(x) then setItems(items) wrong?

options.text: It is the same array, so React sees no change and may not re-render
options.why: React compares the old and new value by identity. Pushing edits the array in place, so both sides are the same object. Use setItems([...items, x]).

options.text: push is not allowed in JavaScript
options.why: push is ordinary JavaScript. The problem is only that React cannot notice it.

options.text: It adds the item twice
options.why: The item is added once. The trouble is that the screen may not show it.

options.text: setItems only takes a function
options.why: It takes a value or a function. Either is fine.

hint: How does React decide whether something changed?

prompt: Which rule must you follow when calling hooks?

options.text: Call them at the top level, never inside a condition or a loop
options.why: React matches hooks to their state by call ORDER. A hook inside an if can change that order between renders, and the state lines up with the wrong hook.

options.text: Call them only inside useEffect
options.why: Hooks are called in the component body. useEffect is itself one of them.

options.text: Call each hook only once per file
options.why: A component may call useState many times. That is normal.

options.text: Call them after the return statement
options.why: Nothing runs after return. They go before it.

hint: React identifies a hook by the order it was called in.
